t.1.139.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While they lay sleeping there, a rākṣasa named Hiḍimba, not far from that forest, had taken refuge in a śāla tree.
t.1.139.2: Cruel, an eater of human flesh, of great valor and great strength, misshapen in form, tawny-eyed, terrible and dreadful to behold, craving flesh and tormented by hunger, he chanced to see them.
t.1.139.4: The wicked eater of human flesh, huge of body and mighty in strength, caught the scent of a human and spoke these words to his sister.
t.1.139.3: With his fingers raised, he scratched himself and shook his rough, matted hair, and, yawning with his huge mouth, looked about again and again.
t.1.139.5: Today, after a long time, a meal dear to my heart has come my way. My tongue pours forth streams of drool and roams all around my mouth.
t.1.139.7: Seizing a human throat and tearing open the vein as well, I shall drink deep of the warm, fresh, frothing blood in abundance.
t.1.139.6: After a long time I shall sink my eight fangs, very sharp at their points and unbearable in their onslaught, into bodies and into rich, tender flesh.
t.1.139.8: Go and find out who these are who lie sleeping here, having taken refuge in the forest. A strong human scent seems to gratify my sense of smell.
t.1.139.9: Kill all these humans and bring them to me. You have nothing to fear from these men sleeping in our territory.
t.1.139.10: Having prepared the flesh of these humans, we two together shall eat it as much as we please; quickly do as I say.
t.1.139.11: Having understood her brother's command, the Rākṣasī, as if in haste, went to the place where the Pāṇḍavas were, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.1.139.12: Having gone there, she saw the Pāṇḍavas lying asleep together with Pṛthā, and Bhīmasena, the unconquered, awake.
t.1.139.13: As soon as she saw Bhīmasena, towering like the trunk of a śāla tree and unequalled in beauty on earth, the rākṣasī was filled with desire for him.
t.1.139.14: This dark, mighty-armed man, with the shoulders of a lion and great splendor, with a neck like a conch shell and eyes like lotuses, would be a fitting husband for me.
t.1.139.15: Never would I carry out my brother's command, bound up as it is with cruelty. Love for a husband is exceedingly strong; affection for a brother is not so.
t.1.139.17: She, able to take any form at will, assumed a most excellent human form and slowly, slowly approached the mighty-armed Bhīmasena.
t.1.139.16: Were these men slain, the satisfaction of my brother and of myself would last only a moment; but by not killing them, I shall rejoice for endless years.
t.1.139.18: Then, like a bashful creeper, adorned with heavenly ornaments, she smiled first and spoke these words to Bhīmasena.
t.1.139.19: From where have you come, and who are you, O bull among men? And who are these men of godlike form who lie sleeping here?
t.1.139.21: He does not know this dense forest, frequented by Rākṣasas; for here dwells an evil-souled Rākṣasa named Hiḍimba.
t.1.139.20: And who is this tall, dark, delicate lady of yours, O sinless one, who, having come to this forest, sleeps as trustingly as if she were in her own house?
t.1.139.23: Having beheld you, whose splendor is like that of a child of the gods, I desire no other husband; this I tell you truly.
t.1.139.22: I was sent by that brother of mine, a rākṣasa of wicked disposition, who wishes to eat the flesh of you all, O you who are like an immortal.
t.1.139.25: I shall save you, mighty-armed one, from the man-eating Rākṣasa. We two shall dwell in mountain fastnesses; become my husband, O sinless one.
t.1.139.24: Knowing this, O knower of dharma, do what is fitting toward me: love me, who love you, my heart and limbs stricken by desire.
t.1.139.26: For I am one who moves through the sky, and I roam wherever I please; attain incomparable delight with me in this place and that.
t.1.139.27: O Rākṣasī, what man with any power at all would now abandon his mother, his eldest brother, and these other younger brothers?
t.1.139.29: Whatever is dear to you, that I shall do; wake all these up. I shall gladly set you free from the man-eating Rākṣasa.
t.1.139.28: For what man like me would go off, as though stricken with desire, leaving these sleeping brothers and our mother as food for a rākṣasa?
t.1.139.30: O Rākṣasī, I will not wake my brothers and my mother, who are sleeping peacefully in the forest, out of fear of your evil-minded brother.
t.1.139.31: For neither Rākṣasas, O timid one, are able to withstand my might, nor men, nor Gandharvas, nor Yakṣas, O lovely-eyed one.
t.1.139.32: Go or stay, good lady, or do whatever you wish; or else, slender-limbed one, send that man-eating brother of yours.
